title: Field-free superconducting diode and tunable vortex dynamics in NbN/FePt stripe-domain heterostructures
authors: Juan C. Zapata, Emilio De Biasi, Martin Sirena, Jeehoon Kim, Nestor Haberkorn
abstract: We demonstrate reconfigurable, field-free superconducting diode behavior in NbN/FePt and NbN/AlN/FePt heterostructures with remanent stripe domains in the FePt layer. NbN films 10 nm thick are capped either directly with FePt or through a thin AlN spacer, which reduces electronic proximity effects while preserving magnetic coupling through stray fields. At zero applied magnetic field, the superconducting diode efficiency reaches approximately 50--60% in NbN/FePt when the stripes are perpendicular to the current and is strongly reduced when they are parallel. The diode effect persists in NbN/AlN/FePt with efficiencies reaching approximately 35--40%, supporting a magnetic origin of the nonreciprocity. We interpret the response as asymmetric vortex transport in the remanent magnetic landscape, with preferential edge vorticity and a Lorentz force that favors inward flux injection or outward motion depending on current polarity. Under applied perpendicular magnetic fields, the interplay between the external field and the magnetic stray fields modifies the flux-flow instability and the apparent instability velocity inferred from transport, with values below those reported for bare NbN films. These results show that stripe-domain ferromagnetic overlayers provide a reconfigurable route to control superconducting nonreciprocity and flux-flow stability in NbN-based heterostructures.
summary: This paper reports on the creation of superconducting diodes in NbN heterostructures using ferromagnetic FePt layers patterned into magnetic stripes. By analyzing the current-voltage characteristics, the authors show that the superconducting nonreciprocity is magnetically controlled, depending on stripe orientation. This work provides a reconfigurable method to manipulate vortex dynamics and superconducting properties using patterned magnetic materials.
main_problem: The research aims to control superconducting nonreciprocity and flux-flow stability in NbN-based heterostructures by leveraging the remanent magnetic fields generated by stripe-domain ferromagnetic overlayers.
main_result: The study demonstrates that the superconducting diode effect is strongly dependent on the orientation of the magnetic stripes, and this nonreciprocity can be maintained or tuned by incorporating an AlN spacer layer.
method: The work combines electrical transport measurements (I-V curves) to probe nonreciprocity with micromagnetic simulations to model the underlying vortex dynamics influenced by stray fields.
model_or_system: The physical system is NbN/FePt and NbN/AlN/FePt heterostructures, where the superconducting properties are coupled to the magnetic stray fields from the patterned FePt layer.
key_observables: Superconducting diode efficiency (nonreciprocity), vortex transport asymmetry, flux-flow instability velocity, and critical temperature ($T_c$).
important_parameters: Stripe domain periodicity ($\approx 100 	ext{ nm}$), spacer thickness (AlN), applied magnetic field strength ($\le 1 	ext{ T}$), and current polarity.
main_assumptions: The nonreciprocity is attributed to asymmetric vortex transport governed by the magnetic stray field landscape, and the AlN spacer successfully decouples electronic proximity effects while preserving magnetic coupling.
figures_summary: The notes suggest figures comparing I-V curves for different stripe orientations and spacer conditions, and potentially showing simulated stray field profiles.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by establishing the physical platform (heterostructures), characterizing the magnetic structure (MFM/XRD), measuring the superconducting response (diode effect), and finally interpreting the results through vortex dynamics models.
why_interesting: The controlled interplay between magnetic texture and superconducting transport offers a novel platform for engineering quantum phenomena, relevant to understanding dissipation and non-equilibrium dynamics in superconducting circuits.
